title: Seven falls in a decade, and what caused each
hook:
On a Monday in March 2020, the Sensex fell so fast in the first minutes of trading that it hit its lower circuit and the exchanges froze trading for three quarters of an hour. Brokers sat watching blank screens. When trading resumed, the selling continued, and by the close the market had suffered its worst single day on record. The next evening the Prime Minister announced a nationwide lockdown.

Every investor remembers a crash like that, and every investor, in the middle of the next one, asks the same question: is this one like that? Is this a dip I should buy, or the start of something much worse?

The honest answer is that nobody knows in real time. But there is a better way to calibrate than gut feel. Every big Indian drawdown of the last decade has a cause you can name, and most of them came from outside India. Lay them side by side, look at what was driving each one and what ended it, and the current fall stops being a mystery and becomes a member of a family. That is what this chapter does.
short: Every Indian drawdown since 2015 has a nameable cause, and most of the big ones started outside India.
The deepest falls came from global shocks, the pandemic above all; India's own events, like demonetisation, sit in the middle of the range.
Oil-and-dollar episodes, 2018 and 2022, produced falls in a fairly narrow band and ended when the external pressure eased, not when Indian growth data improved.
Domestic shocks and credit freezes hurt small caps and consumer stocks far more than the headline index.
The 2026 fall sits inside the 2018 to 2022 band so far, with an unusually calm fear gauge for the size of the oil move.

sections.heading: How deep is deep? Measuring a fall from the top
sections.html:
Start with the ruler. A drawdown is simply how far the market sits below its highest point so far. If the Nifty peaked last January and is now a tenth lower, the drawdown is a tenth, regardless of what happened in between. It is a cruel but honest measure, because it captures exactly what an investor who bought at the top is feeling.

Why not just use the year's return? Because a year can end flat after a deep fall and full recovery in the middle, and the investor who panicked mid-year never got the recovery. Drawdowns measure the experience; returns measure the outcome.

[[fig:1]]

The chart traces the Nifty's distance from its running high, week by week, across the last decade. The line sits at zero whenever the market is making new highs, and dips below whenever it is not. The shaded windows mark the named episodes you will meet below. Notice two things. First, the market spends a surprising share of its life below a previous high: drawdowns are normal, not exceptional. Second, the Covid dip is in a class of its own, a cliff rather than a slope, while the others form a cluster of shallower valleys. The current one, at the far right, sits in that cluster.

Look closely and the time to climb back out varies far more than the depth: the 2020 cliff was climbed in months. Depth tells you how scared to be; the cause tells you how long it might last.

sections.heading: Seven episodes, one table: how to read it
sections.html:
Here is the whole decade on one page. For each episode, we computed from our own data how far the Nifty fell from its prior high inside the window, and what four other gauges did over the same stretch.

[[fig:2]]

Each column is a suspect in the investigation.

  • Brent. The global price of crude. India imports most of its oil, so a rising Brent is a tax on the whole economy.
  • USD/INR. Rupees per dollar. A rising number is a weaker rupee, which shrinks foreign investors' returns in dollars.
  • US ten-year yield. What the American government pays to borrow. When it rises, global money has a safe, attractive home in America, and India has to work harder to keep it.
  • VIX peak. India's fear gauge, built from option prices. High means panic; low means calm, or complacency.

Now read across the rows and the suspects start confessing. In 2018, 2022 and 2026, Brent and US yields were both rising: oil and the dollar squeezing India at the same time. In 2020, oil and US yields both collapsed, and the fear gauge exploded: that was a global panic, not a pressure squeeze. In 2016, the rupee barely moved and the fear gauge stayed the calmest in the table: US yields were rising after Donald Trump's election, but that fall was made in India.

sections.heading: The worst falls were imported
sections.html:
The first pattern is the most uncomfortable for anyone who believes India is a self-contained growth story. The deepest falls of the decade came from abroad: a pandemic that began in China, a currency devaluation in Beijing, a war in Europe, a rate shock in Washington. India's own shocks, demonetisation and the election surprise, sit in the middle and bottom of the range.

Why should a country with a huge domestic economy be so exposed to the world? Because of who owns the shares. Foreign portfolio investors own a large slice of India's biggest companies, and they hold India as one line in an emerging markets portfolio run from London, New York or Singapore. When something scares them about emerging markets in general, they cut the whole basket, and India gets sold along with Brazil, Korea and South Africa, regardless of how Indian companies are doing.

Think of a fund facing redemptions: it sells your favourite stock too, not because anything is wrong with the company, but because it needs cash.

In a global panic, India is not judged on its merits. It is sold because it can be.

There is a second channel too. Global shocks usually arrive with a stronger dollar, and a stronger dollar means a weaker rupee. For a foreign investor, a falling rupee turns a flat Indian stock into a losing position in dollars, which encourages more selling, which weakens the rupee further. It is a loop, and it only breaks when either the global scare passes or the RBI steps in.

The flip side is the good news. Because these falls were driven by things outside India, they tended to end when those things ended, regardless of Indian data. The Covid crash ended when central banks flooded the world with money. The China scare faded when commodity prices stabilised. Watching the external trigger tells you more about the bottom than watching Indian GDP.

sections.heading: Oil and the dollar: India's recurring pressure point
sections.html:
Two episodes in the table look almost like twins: 2018 and 2022. In both, oil was rising, the US Federal Reserve was raising rates, US bond yields were climbing and the rupee was weakening. And in both, the Nifty's worst fall landed in a fairly narrow band, deep enough to hurt but far from a crash.

Here is the chain. Oil goes up and India's import bill swells. The current account deficit, the gap between what India earns from the world and what it pays, widens. More dollars are needed to pay for imports than are coming in, so the rupee weakens. A weaker rupee makes imported oil more expensive still, which pushes up inflation. The RBI then has to choose between letting the rupee slide and raising rates to defend it. Either way, company margins get squeezed and valuations come down.

Now add a rising US yield on top. Foreign investors, already nervous about the rupee, can now earn a handsome, safe return in American government bonds. The opportunity cost of holding Indian shares goes up, and the selling accelerates.

Why did these episodes stop short of a crash? Because the pressure was external and eventually eased. In late 2018 oil fell sharply from its autumn peak and the rupee recovered. In 2022 oil came off its post-invasion highs and Indian markets ended the year a little higher, while much of the world had a terrible year.

That gives a practical rule. In an oil-and-dollar drawdown, the turn rarely comes from good Indian news. It comes when Brent rolls over, when US yields stop rising, and when the rupee stops falling. Those are the three dials to watch, and the 2026 episode is, so far, the same species.

sections.heading: Why domestic shocks hurt small caps far more than the index
sections.html:
India's own shocks look modest in the table, because the table measures the Nifty, which is made of the country's biggest and sturdiest companies. Underneath the index, the story was often much worse.

Take demonetisation. The Nifty's fall was among the shallowest in the table. But the shock landed on cash-dependent businesses: small manufacturers, real estate developers, jewellers, rural consumer demand. Many of the companies most exposed to those sectors were small and mid caps, and their share prices fell much harder than the index.

Or take 2018, the most instructive episode of the decade. On the surface, the Nifty's fall was moderate. But that year small-cap investors lived through a genuine bear market. Part of it was a correction after the euphoric run of 2017, helped along by the return of a long-term capital gains tax on shares in that year's Budget. Then came the real blow: the default of IL&FS, a large infrastructure lender. Mutual funds that held its debt took losses, shunned anyone similar, and the money market froze for non-bank lenders.

Here's why that mattered. Non-bank lenders had been funding much of the lending to small businesses, home buyers and developers, often by borrowing short-term and lending long. When short-term funding dried up, they had to stop lending, and their customers, many of them small companies, lost access to credit. The stress travelled from the lenders' share prices to the borrowers' share prices, and small caps kept falling for more than a year after the index had steadied.

A correction in the index is a weather event. A freeze in credit is a change of climate for small companies, and they suffer for much longer than the headline suggests.

sections.heading: The new shock absorber: Indian savers
sections.html:
Something changed in the second half of the decade: Indian households discovered equity mutual funds. Monthly investment plans, where a fixed sum leaves a salary account and buys fund units automatically, became a habit for millions, and the money kept coming in good months and bad.

That steady stream changed the arithmetic of a sell-off. Before, when foreign investors sold heavily, there were few natural buyers on the other side, so prices had to fall a long way to attract them. Now there is a large, predictable buyer: domestic institutions, mainly mutual funds and insurers, investing the monthly flows of Indian savers. In 2022, foreign investors sold Indian shares on a large scale through much of the year, and domestic institutions more than absorbed it. The Nifty's fall that year was real but contained, much milder than the global sell-off in technology stocks.

Does that make India immune? No. Domestic flows cushion a fall; they do not prevent one. If returns disappoint for long enough, the monthly habit can weaken. And domestic buying supports large caps more than small ones, because that is where most of the money goes.

But it does mean the market's response to foreign selling is no longer what it was before 2020. A heavy run of foreign selling used to be a reliable warning of a deep fall. Today it is worth asking the second question: who is buying what they sell, and how long can they keep it up?

sections.heading: What the fear gauge says, and why calm can mislead
sections.html:
The last column of the table, the VIX peak, is the market's own estimate of how scared it is. The India VIX is calculated from the prices of Nifty options, which work like insurance against big moves. When traders rush to buy protection, those prices jump and the VIX rises. When nobody is worried, protection is cheap and the VIX stays low.

In 2020 the VIX hit a level far above anything else in the decade, a true panic. In most of the other episodes, it peaked at moderately elevated levels. The interesting case is now. For an oil move as large as the one in 2026, the fear gauge has stayed unusually calm.

There are two readings. The generous one: markets have seen oil shocks before, trust the RBI and domestic flows to cushion the fall, and see no reason to pay up for insurance. The less generous one: calm is complacency, and a market that has not panicked has not cleared out its weakest holders. Sharp bottoms have often come with a spike in fear, when the last nervous sellers give up at once.

Neither reading is certain, which is why the VIX is best treated as one input, not a verdict. What it does tell you is that the current drawdown has been an orderly repricing rather than a stampede.

history.title: The devaluation in Beijing
history.story:
In August 2015, China's central bank, then led by Zhou Xiaochuan, unexpectedly devalued the yuan, the biggest move against the dollar in about two decades. Markets read it as a sign that the Chinese economy was weaker than Beijing admitted. Two weeks later came what Chinese state media called Black Monday: Shanghai collapsed and the selling swept the world. The Sensex had its biggest single-day point fall up to that time.

Worse followed in January 2016, when China's newly installed stock market circuit breakers halted trading twice in the first week and were scrapped in embarrassment. Commodity prices collapsed, oil slid to its lowest in more than a decade and every emerging market, India included, was sold as a single asset class.
history.lesson: A growth scare in China reaches India through foreign flows and metal prices, even when Indian companies are doing fine.

history.title: Midnight, and the notes stop working
history.story:
On a November evening in 2016, Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced on television that the two largest banknotes would cease to be legal tender from midnight. The same week, Donald Trump won the US presidential election, rattling markets everywhere. Over the following weeks, queues formed outside every bank and ATM, and small traders lost customers who simply had no cash.

The Nifty dipped, but the damage was concentrated in small caps, real estate and rural consumer companies, whose sales fell sharply for a quarter or two. By the spring the index was making new highs.
history.lesson: Domestic shocks hit small caps and consumption hardest; the index, full of large exporters and banks, often shrugs.

history.title: The Friday DHFL fell off a cliff
history.story:
2018 began with the return of a long-term capital gains tax on shares in Arun Jaitley's Budget and ended in a credit freeze. Through the summer, oil rose and the rupee slid to record lows. Then IL&FS, a giant infrastructure lender, began defaulting on its debt. On a Friday in September, word spread that DSP Mutual Fund had sold commercial paper of the housing lender DHFL at a steep yield. DHFL's shares lost more than half their value during the session. The same morning, Yes Bank crashed after the RBI cut short its founder Rana Kapoor's term. The Sensex plunged intraday before recovering much of the loss.

Within days the government superseded the IL&FS board and installed banker Uday Kotak as chairman. But for small companies that relied on non-bank lenders, credit had dried up, and small caps stayed in a bear market well into the next year.
history.lesson: Liquidity stress turns a routine correction into a small-cap bear market; the index heals first, the small end last.

history.title: The circuit breaker and the lockdown
history.story:
As the virus spread through February and March 2020, global markets went into free fall. On a Monday in March, the Sensex hit its lower circuit within minutes, trading was halted, and the day ended as the worst on record. The next evening Prime Minister Modi announced a nationwide lockdown. Oil prices collapsed so far that, a few weeks later, one US crude contract briefly traded below zero.

Then came the money. The Fed under Jerome Powell cut rates to zero and bought bonds on a vast scale; the RBI under Shaktikanta Das made a large emergency cut and flooded banks with cash. A wave of new retail investors opened trading accounts from home. The recovery was the fastest in the table, and the market was making new highs before the year was out.
history.lesson: Liquidity can repair a crash quickly; the deepest fall of the decade was also the shortest-lived.

history.title: Putin's war and Powell's hikes
history.story:
In the early hours of a February morning in 2022, Russian troops crossed into Ukraine. The Nifty had one of its worst days in years. Oil, wheat and fertiliser prices spiked. Meanwhile, Jerome Powell's Fed, having called inflation transitory a year earlier, began its fastest run of rate hikes in decades, including several jumbo three-quarter-point moves. In May, Das surprised Indian markets with a hike between scheduled meetings.

Foreign investors sold Indian shares heavily for months. Indian technology stocks, which earn in dollars but trade on growth multiples, were hammered. And yet the Nifty held up far better than most markets, because domestic mutual fund flows kept buying what foreigners sold.
history.lesson: Domestic flows capped the damage, which is why a heavy run of foreign selling no longer guarantees a deep fall.

history.title: Two bad days in a bull market
history.story:
On counting day in June 2024, exit polls that had promised a landslide turned out to be wrong, the ruling party lost its single-party majority, and the Nifty had one of its worst days in years. Within weeks it was making new highs. Two months later, the Bank of Japan under Kazuo Ueda raised rates, a weak US jobs report followed, and traders who had borrowed cheap yen to buy assets worldwide rushed to unwind. Japan's Nikkei had its worst day since the 1987 crash, and markets everywhere, India included, tumbled.

Both shocks faded fast. Neither changed Indian earnings, and both arrived in a market with strong underlying momentum.
history.lesson: Event shocks inside a bull market fade quickly when they do not change the economics.

history.title: The strait closes
history.story:
The market began the year at a record. Then, from late February, US and Israeli strikes on Iran turned into a wider war, and the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow channel through which a large share of the world's oil passes, was closed. Oil surged. Foreign money fled emerging markets, the rupee came under pressure, US yields climbed to record highs in our data, and in October the RBI raised rates to defend the currency.

It is, on every gauge in the table, an oil-and-dollar episode: rising Brent, rising US yields, a weaker rupee. And so far the Nifty's fall sits in the same band as 2018 and 2022, not anywhere near 2020.
history.lesson: So far this is a drawdown in the 2018 range; whether it stays there depends on oil and the rupee more than on Indian growth.

today:
The Nifty stands at [[val:nifty]], a little more than a tenth below the record it set at the start of 2026. The fear gauge reads [[val:vix]], calm by the standards of the table. Brent is at [[val:brent]], up [[val:brent_3m]] over three months, the US ten-year yield is at [[val:us10y]], and the rupee is at [[val:usdinr]] per dollar. Foreign investors have sold [[val:fii20]] over the last twenty sessions, and domestic institutions have bought [[val:dii20]], which is the shock absorber at work.

So the current episode looks like 2018 and 2022: an oil-and-dollar squeeze, contained by domestic money. Watch three dials: whether Brent rolls over, whether US yields stop rising, and whether the rupee holds without ever more RBI support. And watch the small-cap end for signs of a credit freeze; that is what turned 2018 from a correction into a bear market.
sowhat:
The current drawdown is in the 2018 range, not the 2020 one, and history says the turn comes when the external pressure eases.

  • Watch oil and the rupee, not the growth data. In oil-and-dollar episodes, the bottom has arrived with relief on those fronts, not with good Indian news.
  • Prefer large, cash-rich companies over small, leveraged ones while money is tight. The index heals first; small caps exposed to tight credit heal last.
  • Be careful with businesses that depend on non-bank lenders for funding or for their customers' credit, such as small developers and vehicle financiers. If credit stress spreads, they feel it first.
  • Remember that domestic flows cushion large caps most. A long or deep drawdown can wear down even that cushion.

What would flip it: a spike in fear alongside a jump in corporate bond spreads or a run on a lender. That would move this episode from the 2018 template towards something more like a credit event, and the small-cap end would take the brunt.
